title: Two charities: perfect charity in the justified, imperfect charity in believing sinners
source_text: XLVIII. Distinguit enim ille inter charitatem proprie dictam, qua Deus super omnia diligitur: & inter charitatem quandam imperfectam, qua Deus gratis quidem & propter se, non tamen super omnia diligitur. Ex ejus mente, prior illa charitas est ipsa justitia nostra; nec reperiri potest, nisi in justificatis, ac proinde non amplius in peccato haerentibus. Posterior vero reperiri potest etiam in peccatoribus, necdum per Dei gratiam a peccatorum suorum reatu liberatis: in quibus per auxilia a Christo subministrata, excitantur quidam actus fidei & dilectionis, per quos peccatores ad recipiendam a Deo justitiam, & peccatorum suorum remissionem disponuntur.
pass_a_gloss: XLVIII. Distinguishes for he between charity properly said, by which God above all things is loved: & between charity a certain imperfect, by which God gratis indeed & on account of himself, not however above all things is loved. Out of his mind, prior that charity is the very justice of ours; nor can it be found, except in the justified, and therefore no longer sticking in sin. But the latter can be found even in sinners, not yet freed by the grace of God from the guilt of their sins: in whom through helps supplied by Christ, certain acts of faith and love are excited, by which sinners are disposed to receiving justice from God, and remission of their sins.
pass_b_english: For he distinguishes charity properly so called, by which God is loved above all, from a certain imperfect charity, by which God is loved freely indeed and for his own sake, yet not above all.

In his mind the first charity is our very righteousness and can be found only in the justified, and so in those no longer stuck in sin. The second can be found even in sinners not yet freed by God's grace from the guilt of their sins. In them, through helps supplied by Christ, certain acts of faith and love are stirred up, by which sinners are disposed to receive righteousness from God and the forgiveness of their sins.

choices.why: The theological virtue by which God is loved for his own sake; Jansenius sets it against cupiditas as the only two loves, so the technical 'charity' is kept rather than 'love'.
